title: PyTorch
name: torch
description: A production-grade, Python-first deep learning and tensor computation package focused on flexible imperative programming, high-performance kernels, and a broad ecosystem for model development and deployment.
summary: PyTorch provides multi-device tensor operations, automatic differentiation, neural network primitives, data loading utilities, compilation tooling, and distributed execution support for research and production systems.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need a fresh tensor built from Python lists or scalars that does not share memory with the source.
tasks.syntax: torch.tensor(data, dtype=None, device=None, requires_grad=False, pin_memory=False)
important_params: data — Python scalar, list, tuple, or ndarray input.
dtype — desired tensor dtype.
device — target device (cpu, cuda).
requires_grad — whether autograd should track the tensor.
pin_memory — pin host memory for faster transfer to CUDA.
tasks.example:
import torch
t = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], dtype=torch.float32)
tasks.use_when: You want an independent Tensor created from Python-native data and do not require zero-copy semantics.
tasks.avoid_when: You need to avoid copies (use torch.as_tensor or torch.from_numpy instead).
gotchas: Always copies Python sequences; does not share memory with the source.
When passed a tensor, behaves like clone().detach(), which can produce a new leaf tensor.
dtype inference may upcast (e.g., ints → long) depending on input; specify dtype to avoid surprises.
pin_memory only affects CPU tensors and is ignored on CUDA.

tasks.task: Create Tensor from Existing Data avoiding copies (`torch.as_tensor`)
tasks.mental_trigger: I need a tensor view over existing numeric data without allocating a duplicate buffer.
tasks.syntax: torch.as_tensor(data, dtype=None, device=None)
important_params: data — array-like (tensor, ndarray, sequence).
dtype — requested dtype (may trigger copy if conversion required).
device — optional device placement for the returned tensor.
tasks.example:
import torch, numpy as np
a = np.array(, dtype=np.float32)[^1][^2][^3]
t = torch.as_tensor(a)
tasks.use_when: Wrapping existing tensors or NumPy arrays for computation without forcing a copy.
tasks.avoid_when: You need a guaranteed new allocation (use torch.tensor), or when input is read-only NumPy array requiring write access.
gotchas: May still copy if dtype/device conversion is necessary.
If input is a torch.Tensor, returns a tensor that may share storage — changes may affect original.
Read-only NumPy arrays may produce undefined behavior if written through the tensor.
as_tensor with nested Python lists will copy.

tasks.task: Create Tensor from NumPy Array with Zero-Copy (`torch.from_numpy`)
tasks.mental_trigger: I need a zero-copy tensor view of an ndarray so updates reflect bidirectionally.
tasks.syntax: torch.from_numpy(ndarray)
important_params: ndarray — NumPy ndarray with compatible dtype and writable memory.
(no other parameters; device/dtype must be handled separately)
tasks.example:
import torch, numpy as np
a = np.array([1.0,2.0], dtype=np.float32)
t = torch.from_numpy(a)
tasks.use_when: Interfacing with NumPy workflows and you need memory-efficient sharing between NumPy and PyTorch.
tasks.avoid_when: Working on CUDA devices (must copy to GPU explicitly) or when the NumPy array is read-only.
gotchas: Returned tensor is CPU-only; moving to CUDA performs a copy.
Writing to tensor will modify ndarray and vice versa; watch for unintended mutations.
Using read-only ndarrays is unsupported and may produce undefined behavior.
Dtype compatibility is limited to supported NumPy dtypes.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need a tensor pre-filled with zeros matching a shape or another tensor.
tasks.syntax:
torch.zeros(*size, dtype=None, device=None, requires_grad=False, pin_memory=False)
torch.zeros_like(input, dtype=None, device=None, requires_grad=False, memory_format=torch.preserve_format)
important_params: size / input — output shape or reference tensor.
dtype — data type.
device — placement device.
requires_grad — autograd tracking flag.
pin_memory / memory_format — host memory pinning and format control.
tasks.example:
import torch
z = torch.zeros(3,4, dtype=torch.float32)
z2 = torch.zeros_like(z)
tasks.use_when: You need deterministic zero initialization or masks with the same shape as existing tensors.
tasks.avoid_when: You need uninitialized memory for performance (use torch.empty).
gotchas: zeros_like will preserve memory format and device by default; explicit device param may allocate copy.
Requires explicit dtype to avoid unexpected integer/float choices.
pin_memory only applies to CPU tensors.
zeros allocates memory; frequent small zeros calls can be costly.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need a tensor of ones matching a shape or another tensor.
tasks.syntax:
torch.ones(*size, dtype=None, device=None, requires_grad=False, pin_memory=False)
torch.ones_like(input, dtype=None, device=None, requires_grad=False, memory_format=torch.preserve_format)
important_params: size / input — shape or reference tensor.
dtype — output dtype.
device — placement device.
requires_grad — autograd flag.
memory_format / pin_memory — memory layout and pin options.
tasks.example:
import torch
o = torch.ones(2,3)
o2 = torch.ones_like(o)
tasks.use_when: Creating constant masks or initialization where ones are required.
tasks.avoid_when: You need uninitialized memory for performance reasons.
gotchas: One-fill writes memory and causes allocation overhead.
ones_like inherits layout/device unless overridden.
Be explicit with dtype to avoid integer vs float surprises.
Frequent allocation in tight loops is costly.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need allocated memory that I will overwrite immediately to avoid initialization cost.
tasks.syntax:
torch.empty(*size, dtype=None, device=None, requires_grad=False, pin_memory=False)
torch.empty_like(input, dtype=None, device=None, requires_grad=False, memory_format=torch.preserve_format)
important_params: size / input — shape or reference.
dtype — dtype of allocated storage.
device — target device.
requires_grad — autograd flag.
memory_format / pin_memory — layout/pinning options.
tasks.example:
import torch
e = torch.empty(3,3, dtype=torch.float32)
tasks.use_when: Preallocating buffers to be filled by computation, reducing allocation overhead.
tasks.avoid_when: You need deterministic initial values (use zeros/ones/full).
gotchas: Contents are uninitialized and may contain arbitrary data; always overwrite before use.
On some backends, empty may still zero memory for safety (backend-dependent).
Using values before assignment yields nondeterministic results.
empty_like inherits metadata and may produce unexpected layout unless controlled.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need a tensor filled with a specific scalar value that matches another tensor's shape or explicit size.
tasks.syntax:
torch.full(size, fill_value, dtype=None, device=None, requires_grad=False, pin_memory=False)
torch.full_like(input, fill_value, dtype=None, device=None, requires_grad=False, memory_format=torch.preserve_format)
important_params: size / input — desired shape or reference tensor.
fill_value — scalar value to fill.
dtype — output dtype.
device — placement device.
requires_grad — autograd behavior.
tasks.example:
import torch
f = torch.full((2,2), 7.0)
tasks.use_when: Initializing bias tensors, masks with non-zero default values, or sentinel arrays.
tasks.avoid_when: You can use broadcasted arithmetic on zeros/ones to compute values without allocation.
gotchas: fill_value will be cast to dtype; ensure compatible dtype to avoid precision loss.
full_like inherits input metadata unless overridden.
Allocation cost similar to zeros/ones.
Using large full allocations can increase memory footprint.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need random or normally distributed tensors or integer samples for sampling indices.
tasks.syntax:
torch.rand(*size, dtype=None, device=None)
torch.randn(*size, dtype=None, device=None)
torch.randint(low, high, size, dtype=None, device=None)
important_params: size — output shape.
dtype — output dtype (rand/randn returns float dtypes).
device — placement device.
low/high (randint) — integer range for sampling.
generator — optional RNG for reproducibility (not always present in shorthand).
tasks.example:
import torch
r = torch.rand(4,4)
n = torch.randn(3)
i = torch.randint(0, 10, (5,))
tasks.use_when: Parameter initialization, data augmentation randomness, stochastic algorithms.
tasks.avoid_when: A deterministic sequence is required; use manual seeding or deterministic generators.
gotchas: Randomness depends on global RNG state unless a generator is provided.
Moving random tensors between devices performs allocation/copy.
Seeding must be managed across processes for distributed reproducibility.
dtype choices affect supported distributions (rand/randn produce floating types).

tasks.mental_trigger: I need a numeric range or evenly spaced sequence as a tensor.
tasks.syntax:
torch.arange(start=0, end, step=1, dtype=None, device=None)
torch.linspace(start, end, steps=100, dtype=None, device=None)
important_params: start, end, step / steps — range specification.
dtype — output dtype.
device — placement device.
inclusive/exclusive behavior — arange end is exclusive.
tasks.example:
import torch
a = torch.arange(0, 10, 2)
l = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, steps=5)
tasks.use_when: Index generation, positional encoding, or parameterized sequences.
tasks.avoid_when: You need multi-dimensional grids (use torch.meshgrid) or non-linear spacing.
gotchas: arange with floating steps may produce rounding differences; prefer linspace for stable counts.
arange end is exclusive; linspace includes both endpoints by definition.
dtype conversion may truncate values unexpectedly.
Large ranges allocate significant memory.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need to verify a tensor's shape, dtype, device, memory layout, and contiguity.
tasks.syntax: tensor.shape, tensor.dtype, tensor.device, tensor.layout, tensor.ndim, tensor.numel(), tensor.stride(), tensor.is_contiguous()
important_params: (accessors; no parameters)
Use tensor.attribute for metadata reads.
tasks.example:
import torch
t = torch.randn(2,3)
print(t.shape, t.dtype, t.device, t.is_contiguous())
tasks.use_when: Validating inputs, selecting code paths based on layout/device, or debugging performance issues.
tasks.avoid_when: You require deep inspection of storage internals beyond public attributes.
gotchas: is_contiguous() depends on memory format and view operations; non-contiguity affects view compatibility.
stride() order indicates how memory is laid out; misinterpreting strides can cause incorrect reshapes.
layout can be sparse or strided; many ops only support strided tensors.
device strings may differ across backends (e.g., 'cuda:0', 'mps').

tasks.mental_trigger: I need a no-copy reshape of a contiguous tensor for indexing or batch adjustments.
tasks.syntax:
tensor.view(*shape)
torch.view_as(tensor, other)
important_params: shape — desired output shape (must be compatible with numel).
(no device/dtype params for view)
Use -1 for automatic dimension inference.
tasks.example:
import torch
t = torch.randn(2,3)
v = t.view(3,2)
tasks.use_when: Reshaping contiguous tensors without allocation for performance and memory efficiency.
tasks.avoid_when: Tensor is non-contiguous due to transposes or slicing (use reshape or contiguous() first).
gotchas: view requires the tensor to be contiguous; otherwise it raises an error.
Using view on a tensor that was created as a view may still be valid only if strides match.
In-place modifications affect both view and base tensor.
Using incorrect shape that mismatches element count raises an error.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need a reshaped tensor regardless of contiguity details.
tasks.syntax:
torch.reshape(input, shape)
torch.reshape_as(input, other)
important_params: input — source tensor.
shape — desired shape (use -1 to infer).
device/dtype not accepted here.
tasks.example:
import torch
t = torch.randn(2,3).t()
r = torch.reshape(t, (3,2))
tasks.use_when: You want a convenient reshape that works across contiguous and non-contiguous tensors.
tasks.avoid_when: You require guaranteed no-copy behavior; use view on known-contiguous tensors.
gotchas: May allocate new memory silently; performance implications if unexpected.
In-place expectations may break if a copy was created.
Strides of the returned tensor may differ from source when a copy occurs.
reshape_as uses other's shape and may trigger copy similarly.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need to collapse batch or spatial dimensions into a single feature dimension.
tasks.syntax: torch.flatten(input, start_dim=0, end_dim=-1)
important_params: input — source tensor.
start_dim — first dimension to flatten.
end_dim — last dimension to flatten.
tasks.example:
import torch
t = torch.randn(2,3,4)
f = torch.flatten(t, start_dim=1)
tasks.use_when: Preparing tensors for linear layers or feature vector extraction.
tasks.avoid_when: You need to preserve original dimensionality; use view/reshape to revert with known shapes.
gotchas: May return a copy if memory layout prevents view.
start_dim/end_dim handling must match tensor rank (negative indexes allowed).
In-place operations on flattened view affect underlying tensor.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need to remove size-1 axes or insert new axes to match expected shapes.
tasks.syntax:
torch.squeeze(input, dim=None)
torch.unsqueeze(input, dim)
important_params: input — source tensor.
dim — specific axis to squeeze/unsqueeze; omit dim to remove all size-1 axes.
tasks.example:
import torch
t = torch.randn(3,1,4)
s = torch.squeeze(t, 1)
u = torch.unsqueeze(s, 1)
tasks.use_when: Preparing tensors for broadcasting, ensuring batch dimensions, or aligning shapes.
tasks.avoid_when: Attempting to squeeze non-singleton dimensions (raises error if specific dim mismatched).
gotchas: squeeze without dim removes all size-1 axes and may change intended semantics.
Unsqueeze indices follow Python indexing rules; negative dims allowed.
Both are usually views; in-place expectations affect original tensor.
Using squeeze on tensors where dim !=1 raises error.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need to swap or reorder axes for convolution, linearization, or layout conversion.
tasks.syntax:
torch.transpose(input, dim0, dim1)
torch.permute(input, dims)
important_params: dim0, dim1 / dims — axis indices to swap or the full permutation tuple.
input — source tensor.
tasks.example:
import torch
t = torch.randn(2,3,4)
p = torch.permute(t, (0,2,1))
s = torch.transpose(t, 1, 2)
tasks.use_when: Converting between channel-first/channel-last layouts or swapping batch/spatial dims.
tasks.avoid_when: Expecting contiguous memory subsequently; call contiguous() if a contiguous buffer is required.
gotchas: Permuted tensors are often non-contiguous; many ops require contiguity.
Subsequent view() calls will fail unless tensor is contiguous.
In-place operations can be invalid or change underlying storage unexpectedly.
Repeated permutations can increase code complexity and mistake risk.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need a contiguous tensor before calling an API that requires contiguous input.
tasks.syntax: tensor.contiguous(memory_format=torch.contiguous_format)
important_params: memory_format — memory layout hint.
(no device/dtype params)
tasks.example:
import torch
t = torch.randn(2,3).t()
tc = t.contiguous()
tasks.use_when: Preparing inputs for C/C++ extensions or kernels expecting contiguous buffers.
tasks.avoid_when: You do not need a contiguous buffer — avoid unnecessary copies.
gotchas: May allocate a new buffer and copy data, causing performance overhead.
memory_format influences layout and can affect downstream views/strides.
Calling contiguous repeatedly on already-contiguous tensors is a no-op but adds call overhead.
In-place expectations may be invalid if a copy was made.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need an independent copy of tensor contents to mutate without affecting the original.
tasks.syntax: tensor.clone(memory_format=torch.preserve_format)
important_params: memory_format — layout of the cloned tensor.
(no device/dtype parameters)
tasks.example:
import torch
t = torch.randn(2,3)
c = t.clone()
tasks.use_when: Safely copying tensors prior to in-place operations or cross-scope mutations.
tasks.avoid_when: You want zero-copy views (use view/reshape) or when shallow copy semantics suffice.
gotchas: clone always allocates new storage, which increases memory usage.
Clone of a non-contiguous tensor may produce a contiguous copy depending on memory_format.
clone preserves requires_grad on the returned tensor by default (autograd semantics apply).
Large clones can cause peak memory pressure.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need to merge a list of tensors along a shared dimension into one tensor.
tasks.syntax: torch.cat(tensors, dim=0, *, out=None)
important_params: tensors — iterable of tensors with matching shapes except at dim.
dim — axis along which to concatenate.
out — optional output tensor for storage.
tasks.example:
import torch
a = torch.ones(2,3)
b = torch.zeros(1,3)
c = torch.cat([a,b], dim=0)
tasks.use_when: Collating minibatches, merging features, and combining outputs from parallel branches.
tasks.avoid_when: You can use stacking for adding a new dimension, or preallocate and write into buffers to avoid repeated concatenations.
gotchas: All tensors must be on the same device and have compatible dtypes.
Concatenation allocates new memory proportional to the combined size.
Frequent repeated concatenation in loops is expensive; prefer list accumulation + single cat.
Non-contiguous inputs may cause extra copies during cat.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need to assemble a list of tensors into a single tensor where each input becomes a slice along a new axis.
tasks.syntax: torch.stack(tensors, dim=0, *, out=None)
important_params: tensors — sequence of tensors with identical shapes.
dim — index at which to insert the new axis.
out — optional output tensor.
tasks.example:
import torch
a = torch.tensor()[^2][^1]
b = torch.tensor()[^3][^4]
s = torch.stack([a,b], dim=0)  \# shape (2,2)
tasks.use_when: Creating batched tensors from separate elements or assembling per-sample outputs.
tasks.avoid_when: You want to concatenate along an existing axis (use torch.cat).
gotchas: All inputs must have identical shapes and dtypes.
Stack always allocates new memory.
Inputs must be on the same device.
Frequent stacking can be less efficient than preallocating a buffer.

tasks.task: Split Tensor into Chunks or Sections (`torch.split` / `torch.chunk`)
tasks.mental_trigger: I need to divide a tensor into parts either by explicit sizes or equal chunks.
tasks.syntax:
torch.split(tensor, split_size_or_sections, dim=0)
torch.chunk(tensor, chunks, dim=0)
important_params: split_size_or_sections / chunks — sizes or number of parts.
dim — axis to split along.
tasks.example:
import torch
t = torch.arange(8)
parts = torch.split(t, )[^5][^3]
tasks.use_when: Sharding workloads, mini-batching, or dividing data for parallel pipelines.
tasks.avoid_when: You require complex non-contiguous slicing patterns; consider index_select or advanced indexing.
gotchas: split with uneven sections behaves as specified; chunk with non-divisible sizes yields smaller last chunk.
May return views which share storage — mutating outputs may affect the original.
All resulting tensors must be used carefully with device and dtype considerations.
Large number of small splits can cause overhead.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need fine-grained selection or scatter semantics using index tensors.
tasks.syntax:
torch.index_select(input, dim, index)
torch.gather(input, dim, index)
torch.scatter(input, dim, index, src)
torch.take_along_dim(input, indices, dim)
important_params: input — source tensor.
dim — axis for operation.
index / indices — integer tensors specifying positions.
src — source values for scatter.
tasks.example:
import torch
t = torch.tensor([,])[^4][^1][^2][^3]
idx = torch.tensor()[^1]
g = torch.gather(t, 1, idx.unsqueeze(0))
tasks.use_when: Implementing advanced indexing, batched gather operations, or scatter-accumulate patterns.
tasks.avoid_when: Simple slicing or boolean indexing suffices; these APIs are for index-driven operations.
gotchas: Shapes of index and input must align per API contract — mismatches raise errors.
gather/scatter semantics differ subtly; gather reads from input, scatter writes into output.
scatter may be in-place and can overwrite data unexpectedly.
take_along_dim introduced for clearer semantics in some versions — check compatibility.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need to compute arithmetic between tensors or update tensors in-place to reduce allocations.
tasks.syntax:
torch.add(input, other, *, out=None) / torch.Tensor.add
torch.add_(tensor, other)  \# in-place variant
(similar for sub, mul, div and their in-place counterparts)
important_params: input/other — operands (tensor or scalar).
out — optional preallocated output.
alpha / broadcasting rules — scale factor for some ops.
dtype promotion behavior — implicit casting rules.
tasks.example:
import torch
a = torch.ones(3)
b = torch.tensor()[^2][^3][^1]
c = a + b
a.add_(b)
tasks.use_when: Basic arithmetic, incremental updates to buffers, and avoiding intermediate allocations.
tasks.avoid_when: Autograd history must be preserved in specific ways — in-place ops can complicate gradient computation.
gotchas: In-place ops can break autograd when they modify values needed for gradient computation.
Broadcasting rules may cause implicit expansion leading to larger allocations.
Dtype promotion can silently change dtype (e.g., int + float → float).
Using out= with overlapping memory may produce undefined behavior.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need efficient dense matrix or batched matrix multiplication on tensors.
tasks.syntax:
torch.matmul(input, other)
torch.mm(mat1, mat2)  \# 2-D only
torch.bmm(batch1, batch2)  \# 3-D batched matmul
important_params: input/mat1/batch1 — left operand.
other/mat2/batch2 — right operand.
out — optional preallocated output in some variants.
dtype/device — implicit from inputs.
tasks.example:
import torch
a = torch.randn(3,4)
b = torch.randn(4,5)
c = torch.matmul(a,b)
tasks.use_when: Linear algebra, dense layers, and batched linear operations.
tasks.avoid_when: Sparse-dense matmul needed; use specialized sparse APIs.
gotchas: Dimension mismatch errors are common if ranks/shapes are incorrect.
matmul semantics differ across 1-D/2-D/ND inputs (e.g., vector-matrix behavior).
Data layout and dtype (float16 vs float32) affect kernel availability and performance.
Large batched matmul may require memory planning to avoid OOM.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need sums, means, extrema, or argmax across dimensions for metrics or pooling.
tasks.syntax:
torch.sum(input, dim=None, keepdim=False)
torch.mean(input, dim=None, keepdim=False)
torch.max(input, dim=None, keepdim=False)
torch.min(input, dim=None, keepdim=False)
torch.argmax(input, dim=None, keepdim=False)
important_params: input — tensor to reduce.
dim — axis or axes for reduction.
keepdim — whether to retain reduced dims.
dtype — optional accumulation dtype.
tasks.example:

s = torch.sum(t, dim=1)

tasks.avoid_when: You need elementwise outputs; reductions change tensor rank.
gotchas: Accumulation dtype can overflow for narrow integer types; specify dtype for safety.
max/min return values and indices variants have different signatures.
Reductions on non-contiguous tensors work but may incur copies.
argmax returns indices with dtype torch.long.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need to pick values by condition or build coordinate matrices for spatial operations.
tasks.syntax:
torch.where(condition, x, y)
torch.meshgrid(*tensors, indexing='xy')
important_params: condition — boolean tensor.
x, y — tensors or scalars for selection.
tensors — 1-D tensors for meshgrid.
indexing — 'xy' or 'ij' to control axis ordering.
tasks.example:
import torch
cond = torch.tensor([True, False])
out = torch.where(cond, torch.tensor(), torch.tensor())[^1]
x = torch.linspace(0,1,3)
X,Y = torch.meshgrid(x, x, indexing='xy')
tasks.use_when: Masking, conditional computation, or building coordinate frames for image ops.
tasks.avoid_when: You only need boolean indexing (use masked_select) or simple broadcasting arithmetic.
gotchas: where requires shapes compatible for broadcasting.
meshgrid indexing parameter changes axis order; mismatches cause subtle bugs.
where with mixed dtypes may upcast results.
Large meshgrids allocate O(N^2) memory for 2D cases.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need to broadcast a smaller tensor to a larger shape without copying data.
tasks.syntax:
tensor.expand(*sizes)
tensor.expand_as(other)
important_params: sizes — desired expanded shape (must be compatible via broadcasting).
other — tensor to match shape.
tasks.example:
import torch
t = torch.tensor()[^3][^2][^1]
e = t.expand(3,3)
tasks.use_when: Broadcasting constants or parameters across batch dimensions cheaply.
tasks.avoid_when: You need a real allocated tensor (use repeat) or need to write to the expanded tensor.
gotchas: Expanded tensors are **views** with stride 0 in expanded dims; in-place writes are not allowed.
expand cannot add new memory-backed dimensions that require distinct storage.
Using expand on non-broadcast-compatible shapes raises errors.
Some ops do not accept expanded tensors as writable outputs.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need a fully materialized repeated tensor for indexing or writable buffers.
tasks.syntax: tensor.repeat(*sizes)
important_params: sizes — repeat multipliers for each dimension.
tasks.example:
import torch
t = torch.tensor()[^2][^1]
r = t.repeat(2,1)  \# shape (2,2)
tasks.use_when: You require explicit allocation of repeated patterns or writable repeated data.
tasks.avoid_when: You only need read-only broadcast behavior (use expand).
gotchas: repeat allocates memory proportional to the repeated size — can be large.
Repeated data is independent copies; modifying result does not affect source.
Using repeat with large multipliers may cause OOM.
repeat requires matching ranks or prepending singleton dims as needed.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need to place tensors on a specific device or change dtype/precision for compute.
tasks.syntax:
tensor.to(device=None, dtype=None, non_blocking=False, copy=False)
tensor.cpu(), tensor.cuda(device=None, non_blocking=False), tensor.to(torch.float32), tensor.half(), tensor.to(torch.bfloat16)
important_params: device — target device (cpu, cuda:X, mps).
dtype — target dtype (torch.float32, torch.float16, torch.bfloat16, etc.).
non_blocking — whether copy may be asynchronous for pinned memory.
copy — force a copy even if already matching dtype/device.
tasks.example:
import torch
t = torch.randn(3,3)
g = t.cuda()
f = g.float()
h = f.to('cpu', non_blocking=True)
tasks.use_when: Preparing tensors for device-specific computation, optimizing memory footprint with lower precision, or converting for interoperability.
tasks.avoid_when: Automatic implicit device moves are cheaper for prototyping but expensive in production; prefer explicit placement.
gotchas: to(cuda) performs a device transfer that allocates GPU memory; ensure device has capacity.
non_blocking only helps when source is pinned host memory.
Casting to lower precision can change numerical behavior and support of kernels.
Using .cuda() without specifying device in multi-GPU contexts can target unexpected GPU.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need PyTorch to track operations on a newly created input or weight tensor so I can compute derivatives during the backward pass.
tasks.syntax:
torch.tensor(data, requires_grad=True, dtype=None, device=None)  
# Or setting the attribute post-creation:  
tensor.requires_grad = True
important_params: requires_grad (bool): Whether operations on this tensor should be recorded in the computation graph. Default is False.
dtype (torch.dtype, optional): Datatype of the tensor. Floating point and complex types support gradient tracking; integer types do not.
device (torch.device, optional): Hardware device (e.g., 'cpu', 'cuda').
tasks.example:
import torch

# Enable tracking during tensor creation  
x = torch.tensor([1.5, 2.5], requires_grad=True)

# Compute downstream result  
y = x ** 2 + 3.0  
z = y.mean()

print(f"x requires_grad: {x.requires_grad}")  
print(f"z requires_grad: {z.requires_grad}")  
print(f"z grad_fn: {z.grad_fn}")
tasks.use_when:
Initializing trainable model parameters manually.
Creating input tensors when computing input-level gradients (e.g., adversarial attacks, saliency maps).
Converting non-differentiable data into differentiable computational roots.
tasks.avoid_when:
Loading frozen pretrained weights where parameters should not be updated.
Setting up inference or validation loops where tracking wastes memory and compute.
Working with integer or boolean tensors, which cannot track gradients.
gotchas: Assigning requires_grad=True on non-floating-point tensors (e.g., torch.int64) raises a RuntimeError.
Changing .requires_grad = True in-place on a non-leaf tensor that already has history is disallowed; use .requires_grad_() or recreate the tensor.
Any operation involving at least one input with requires_grad=True produces an output with requires_grad=True.

tasks.mental_trigger: I want to freeze specific layers or weights in-place so they no longer update during backpropagation.
tasks.syntax: tensor.requires_grad_(requires_grad=True)
important_params: requires_grad (bool): If False, disables gradient tracking for this tensor in-place. Default is True.
tasks.example:
import torch

# Initialize weight tensor with tracking enabled  
weight = torch.randn(3, 3, requires_grad=True)

# Freeze weight tensor for fine-tuning  
weight.requires_grad_(False)

print(f"Weight tracking enabled: {weight.requires_grad}")

# Verify downstream graph inclusion  
output = weight @ torch.randn(3, 1)  
print(f"Output has grad_fn: {output.grad_fn is not None}")
tasks.use_when:
Freezing backbone layers during transfer learning or multi-stage model training.
Disabling gradients on specific model parameters dynamically during alternate optimization steps (e.g., GAN training).
tasks.avoid_when:
Disabling tracking for an entire forward block; use torch.no_grad() or torch.inference_mode() context managers instead.
Calling on intermediate tensors inside a active computation graph; in-place modification of non-leaf tensors with history will raise an error.
gotchas: requires_grad_(False) on a leaf tensor prevents future operations from building graph links, but it does not erase previously recorded gradients stored in .grad.
Attempting requires_grad_(False) on a tensor generated by an operation (non-leaf) raises a RuntimeError: *"you can only change requires_grad flags of leaf variables"*.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need to construct primary input or parameter tensors that will hold accumulated gradients when .backward() completes.
tasks.syntax:
torch.tensor(data, requires_grad=True)  
# Or creating from factory functions:  
torch.ones(size, requires_grad=True)  
torch.randn(size, requires_grad=True)
important_params: data / size: Input data array or structural shape.
requires_grad (bool): Set to True to mark the created tensor as a root node that tracks gradients.
dtype (torch.dtype, optional): Floating-point or complex type.
device (torch.device, optional): Hardware target.
tasks.example:
import torch

# Explicitly create a leaf tensor via factory function  
weights = torch.randn(5, 5, requires_grad=True)

# Derive a non-leaf tensor through an operation  
activations = weights * 2.0

print(f"weights.is_leaf: {weights.is_leaf}, grad_fn: {weights.grad_fn}")  
print(f"activations.is_leaf: {activations.is_leaf}, grad_fn: {activations.grad_fn}")
tasks.use_when:
Manually defining custom model parameters outside of torch.nn.Parameter.
Defining optimization targets for custom optimization solvers or input space optimization.
tasks.avoid_when:
Constructing intermediate variables within network forward passes; operations automatically create non-leaf nodes.
Processing input data batches where gradients for inputs are not required.
gotchas: Any tensor created directly by the user (not returned by an operation) is a leaf tensor. If requires_grad=True, it accumulates .grad.
A tensor created via an operation (e.g., a = b + c) is not a leaf tensor. Its gradients are cleared after .backward() unless retain_grad() is called.
Performing an in-place operation on a leaf tensor that requires grad will raise a RuntimeError during backward pass.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need to debug why gradients are missing or why memory is leaking by checking if a tensor is a leaf node and tracking gradients.
tasks.syntax:
tensor.requires_grad  # Returns bool  
tensor.is_leaf        # Returns bool  
tensor.grad_fn        # Returns Node object or None
important_params: None (property accesses).
tasks.example:
import torch

# Create a leaf tensor  
x = torch.tensor([2.0], requires_grad=True)

# Derive non-leaf tensors  
y = x ** 3  
z = y + 5

def inspect_tensor(name, t):  
    print(f"[{name}] requires_grad={t.requires_grad}, is_leaf={t.is_leaf}, grad_fn={t.grad_fn}")

tasks.use_when:
Debugging NoneType issues when reading .grad after backward().
Diagnosing memory leaks caused by unwanted graph construction on intermediate variables.
Verifying model layer freezing logic in test suites.
tasks.avoid_when: Inside performance-critical inner loops where overhead from property access or string logging is undesirable.
gotchas: All tensors with requires_grad=False are leaf tensors by definition (is_leaf=True), even if derived from operations.
A tensor created via x.detach() creates a new leaf tensor with requires_grad=False.
Intermediate tensors have is_leaf=False and requires_grad=True. Their .grad will remain None after backward() unless retain_grad() was called prior to backpropagation.

tasks.mental_trigger: I have computed a scalar loss value and need to backpropagate derivatives through the entire neural network graph.
tasks.syntax: tensor.backward(gradient=None, retain_graph=None, create_graph=False, inputs=None)
important_params: gradient (torch.Tensor, optional): Gradient vector matching tensor shape if tensor is non-scalar. Required for vector outputs; defaults to torch.tensor(1.0) for scalars.
retain_graph (bool, optional): If False, graph buffers are freed after backward pass. Must be set to True if invoking backward multiple times on the same graph.
create_graph (bool, optional): If True, creates a graph of the backward operations, enabling higher-order derivative computation (e.g., Hessian-vector products). Default is False.
inputs (sequence of Tensor, optional): Leaf tensors whose .grad attributes will be populated. Non-target tensors are bypassed.
tasks.example:
import torch

# Define leaf variables  
w = torch.tensor([2.0, 3.0], requires_grad=True)  
x = torch.tensor([4.0, 5.0])

# Compute forward loss (scalar)  
loss = (w * x).sum()

# Compute gradients  
loss.backward()

print(f"w.grad: {w.grad}")  # d(loss)/dw = x = [4.0, 5.0]
tasks.use_when:
Standard training iteration step to calculate parameter gradients from a scalar loss.
Computing Jacobians or custom gradient steps by supplying explicit vector values to gradient.
tasks.avoid_when:
Computing gradients for specific outputs without mutating .grad attributes; use torch.autograd.grad instead.
Running inference or evaluation loops.
gotchas: Calling .backward() on a non-scalar tensor without providing the gradient argument raises a RuntimeError: *"grad can be implicitly created only for scalar outputs"*.
Re-executing .backward() without setting retain_graph=True raises a RuntimeError stating that the graph buffers have already been freed.
Gradients accumulate into .grad buffers via addition; failing to zero gradients between iterations leads to incorrect updates.

tasks.mental_trigger: I want to calculate derivatives for specific tensors without touching the .grad attributes or affecting the optimizer's state.
tasks.syntax:
torch.autograd.grad(  
    outputs,  
    inputs,  
    grad_outputs=None,  
    retain_graph=None,  
    create_graph=False,  
    allow_unused=False  
)
important_params: outputs (Tensor or sequence of Tensor): Tensors whose derivatives are taken.
inputs (Tensor or sequence of Tensor): Tensors with respect to which gradients are computed.
grad_outputs (Tensor or sequence of Tensor, optional): Vector for vector-Jacobian product. Mandatory if outputs are non-scalar.
retain_graph (bool, optional): Retains graph for additional backward passes.
create_graph (bool, optional): Enables higher-order gradient graphs.
allow_unused (bool, optional): If False, raises error if specified input is not part of the graph. Default is False.
tasks.example:
import torch

x = torch.tensor([3.0], requires_grad=True)  
y = x ** 3

# Compute dy/dx directly  
grads = torch.autograd.grad(outputs=y, inputs=x, create_graph=True)[0]  
print(f"First derivative (dy/dx): {grads.item()}")

# Compute second derivative d2y/dx2 using returned gradient node  
second_grad = torch.autograd.grad(outputs=grads, inputs=x)[0]  
print(f"Second derivative (d2y/dx2): {second_grad.item()}")

# Verify leaf grad remains untouched  
print(f"x.grad is None: {x.grad is None}")
tasks.use_when:
Calculating higher-order derivatives (e.g., physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), penalty loss terms like WGAN-GP).
Computing Jacobians or sensitivity metrics without side effects on optimizer parameters.
tasks.avoid_when: Standard training steps where loss.backward() and optimizer.step() are standard.
gotchas: If an input in inputs has no functional connection to outputs and allow_unused=False (default), PyTorch raises a RuntimeError.
Intermediate graph nodes created without create_graph=True cannot be differentiated again.

tasks.mental_trigger: My model causes Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors at my target batch size, so I need to run multiple smaller passes and sum gradients before stepping the optimizer.
tasks.syntax:
# Iterative loop behavior  
loss = loss / accumulation_steps  
loss.backward()  # Adds gradients into existing .grad buffers
important_params: accumulation_steps (int): Number of micro-batches processed prior to triggering optimizer.step() and optimizer.zero_grad().
tasks.example:
import torch  
import torch.nn as nn

model = nn.Linear(10, 2)  
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.01)  
accumulation_steps = 4

# Zero gradients initially  
optimizer.zero_grad()

for i in range(accumulation_steps):  
    dummy_input = torch.randn(8, 10)  
    output = model(dummy_input)  
    loss = output.sum() / accumulation_steps  # Normalize loss scale  
      
    # Accumulate gradients (does NOT overwrite .grad)  
    loss.backward()

# Perform parameter update after accumulating 4 micro-batches  
optimizer.step()  
optimizer.zero_grad()  
print("Accumulation cycle complete. Gradients applied and cleared.")
tasks.use_when:
Training large language models, vision transformers, or high-resolution vision pipelines on memory-constrained GPUs.
Matching baseline paper performance that requires multi-GPU batch sizes on single-card workstations.
tasks.avoid_when: Operating within sufficient hardware memory bounds; standard batch processing exhibits better GPU tensor core utilization.
gotchas: Forgetting to scale/normalize the loss (loss / accumulation_steps) results in effective gradient magnitudes scaling linearly with accumulation step count, causing optimization divergence.
Calling optimizer.zero_grad() inside the micro-batch loop erases accumulated gradients prematurely.
Batch normalization layers behave differently when batch sizes shrink during micro-batch splits; switch to GroupNorm or LayerNorm for gradient-accumulated training.

tasks.task: Reset Gradients Before Backward (optimizer.zero_grad, Tensor.grad = None)
tasks.mental_trigger: I am starting a new training iteration and must reset parameter gradients to zero before computing the next backward pass.
tasks.syntax:
optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)  
# Or manually clearing a single tensor:  
tensor.grad = None
important_params: set_to_none (bool): If True, sets parameter .grad attributes to None instead of filling existing tensors with zeros. Default in modern PyTorch best practices is True.
tasks.example:
import torch  
import torch.nn as nn

layer = nn.Linear(5, 1)  
x = torch.randn(2, 5)

# Step 1: Perform first backward  
loss1 = layer(x).sum()  
loss1.backward()  
print(f"Grad before reset: {layer.weight.grad[0, :2]}")

# Step 2: Reset using set_to_none=True  
layer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)  
print(f"Grad after zero_grad: {layer.weight.grad}")

# Step 3: Perform second backward cleanly  
loss2 = layer(x).sum()  
loss2.backward()  
print(f"Grad after second backward: {layer.weight.grad[0, :2]}")
tasks.use_when:
At the beginning or end of every training iteration loop.
Prior to running auxiliary loss backward passes that require isolated gradient tracking.
tasks.avoid_when: Performing multi-step gradient accumulation across micro-batches (where clearing should occur only after the optimizer step).
gotchas: Forgetting to reset gradients causes new gradients to sum with previous steps, causing gradient explosion within a few iterations.
Using set_to_none=False allocates and retains zero-filled memory buffers for .grad, consuming unnecessary VRAM between backward passes.

tasks.mental_trigger: I want to inspect, log, clip, or analyze computed gradient magnitudes for specific model parameters after backpropagation.
tasks.syntax: gradient_tensor = tensor.grad
important_params: None (property access).

import torch

x = torch.tensor([2.0, -3.0], requires_grad=True)  
y = (x ** 2).sum()

y.backward()

# Access computed gradient (d(y)/dx = 2x)  
x_grad = x.grad

print(f"Tensor values: {x}")  
print(f"Computed grads: {x_grad}")  
print(f"Grad norm: {torch.linalg.vector_norm(x_grad):.4f}")
tasks.use_when:
Implementing custom gradient clipping, logging metrics to TensorBoard/Weights\&Biases, or analyzing exploding/vanishing gradient problems.
Building custom optimization routines outside standard torch.optim classes.
tasks.avoid_when: Attempting to retrieve gradients for intermediate (non-leaf) tensors without first calling retain_grad() (will return None).
gotchas: Modifying .grad in-place without wrapping operations in with torch.no_grad(): can cause unexpected autograd state behavior.
If .backward() has not been called, or if requires_grad=False, .grad returns None. Accessing methods on None raises an AttributeError.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need to inspect gradients on intermediate layer activations (non-leaf tensors) for debugging or custom loss calculation.
tasks.syntax: intermediate_tensor.retain_grad()
important_params: None.
tasks.example:
import torch

x = torch.tensor([3.0], requires_grad=True)  # Leaf tensor  
y = x ** 2                                   # Non-leaf intermediate tensor  
z = y * 5                                    # Non-leaf output tensor

# Instruct PyTorch not to discard y's gradient buffer  
y.retain_grad()

z.backward()

print(f"x.grad (leaf): {x.grad}")  
print(f"y.grad (intermediate retained): {y.grad}")  
print(f"z.grad (output non-retained): {z.grad}")
tasks.use_when:
Feature map visualization techniques (e.g., Grad-CAM) requiring activation-level gradients.
Debugging vanishing or exploding gradients deep inside complex network architectures.
tasks.avoid_when: Running standard production training loops where intermediate activation gradients are unnecessary; retain_grad increases VRAM allocation.

Retaining gradients prevents the garbage collection of intermediate buffers during backpropagation, leading to higher VRAM usage.

tasks.task: Detect Gradient Availability and Missing Gradients
tasks.mental_trigger: My model parameters aren't updating because param.grad is None. I need to diagnose where the graph broke.
tasks.syntax:
if tensor.grad is None:  
    # Diagnose graph connectivity and settings  
    has_tracking = tensor.requires_grad  
    is_leaf_node = tensor.is_leaf  
    has_creator = tensor.grad_fn is not None
important_params: None.
tasks.example:
import torch

x = torch.tensor([2.0], requires_grad=True)

# Graph Break Scenario: Convert to numpy accidentally or usage of non-differentiable ops  
intermediate = x.detach() * 3  # detached!  
loss = intermediate.sum()

if loss.requires_grad:  
    loss.backward()  
else:  
    print("Graph broken! Loss does not track gradients.")

print(f"x.grad status: {x.grad}")  # Returns None because chain was broken
tasks.use_when:
Automated unit tests testing custom layer forward implementations.
Debugging frozen components or broken backward flows during novel model development.
tasks.avoid_when: Production operational passes (adds unnecessary runtime assert checks).
gotchas: Intermediate tensors (is_leaf=False) naturally return .grad = None after .backward() unless retain_grad() is explicitly called. This is expected behavior, not a broken graph.
Non-differentiable operations (e.g., torch.argmax, indexing with boolean masks, integer casting) silently break gradient history tracking.

tasks.mental_trigger: I want to modify, clip, scale, or log a specific tensor's gradient on-the-fly during the backward pass without altering model source code.
tasks.syntax:
handle = tensor.register_hook(hook_fn)  
# hook_fn signature:  
# hook_fn(grad) -\> Tensor or None
important_params: hook_fn (Callable): A user-defined callback that accepts grad as an argument. It can return None (leaving gradient unmodified) or a new Tensor replacing the computed gradient.
tasks.example:
import torch

x = torch.tensor([2.0, -4.0], requires_grad=True)  
y = x ** 2  
z = y.sum()

# Define a hook that clips gradients to positive values only  
def clamp_grad_hook(grad):  
    return torch.clamp(grad, min=0.0)

# Register hook on intermediate tensor y  
handle = y.register_hook(clamp_grad_hook)

z.backward()

print(f"x.grad after hook intervention: {x.grad}")

# Clean up hook  
handle.remove()

Implementing custom gradient modifications (e.g., Gradient Reversal Layers in domain adaptation networks).
Injecting localized gradient logging, telemetry, or debugging probes.
tasks.avoid_when: Global parameter gradient clipping; use torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_ or optimizer wrappers instead.
gotchas: Returning a tensor with a different shape or dtype from hook_fn causes a RuntimeError during backward propagation.
In-place modification of the incoming grad argument inside the hook can corrupt state; always return a modified copy if altering values.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need to inspect, record, or modify intermediate feature representations inside a neural network without modifying its forward() codebase.
tasks.syntax:
handle = module.register_forward_hook(hook_fn, always_call=False)  
# hook_fn signature:  
# hook_fn(module, args, output) -\> Tensor or None
important_params: hook_fn (Callable): Function called with (module, input_args, output). Returning a value overrides the layer output.
always_call (bool, optional): If True, hook executes even if an exception occurs during forward pass. Default is False.
tasks.use_when:
Extracting intermediate feature representations for downstream tasks, perceptual losses, or activation logging.
Implementing network visualization and neural architecture analysis tools.
tasks.avoid_when: Tensors returned by forward hooks intended for feature extraction should be detached (.detach()); otherwise, unneeded autograd graphs stay pinned in VRAM.
gotchas: Modifying returned output in-place inside a forward hook affects all subsequent layers down the computational line.
Forgetting to call handle.remove() when hooks are created dynamically within loops leads to memory leaks and multiple calls per step.

tasks.mental_trigger: I want to monitor or adjust gradients flowing through an entire nn.Module layer during backward execution.
tasks.syntax:
handle = module.register_full_backward_hook(hook_fn)  
# hook_fn signature:  
# hook_fn(module, grad_input, grad_output) -\> tuple(Tensor) or None
important_params: hook_fn (Callable): Function signature accepting (module, grad_input, grad_output). Returning a tuple replaces input gradients flowing upstream.
tasks.example:
import torch  
import torch.nn as nn

layer = nn.Linear(3, 2)

def backward_hook(module, grad_input, grad_output):  
    print(f"[Backward Hook] Module: {module.__class__.__name__}")  
    print(f"  grad_output shape: {grad_output[0].shape}")  
    print(f"  grad_input (weight) shape: {grad_input[1].shape}")

handle = layer.register_full_backward_hook(backward_hook)

x = torch.randn(1, 3, requires_grad=True)  
out = layer(x)  
loss = out.sum()  
loss.backward()

handle.remove()
tasks.use_when: Auditing gradient flow, exploding/vanishing gradient metrics per module, or implementing specialized gradient modification layers.
tasks.avoid_when:
Modifying individual tensor gradients; register_hook on specific tensors is safer and simpler.
Using deprecated register_backward_hook which had broken behavior on complex architectures with multiple inputs/outputs.
gotchas: Deprecated register_backward_hook should never be used in PyTorch 2.x; use register_full_backward_hook exclusively.
Arguments grad_input and grad_output are tuples. Unpacking them incorrectly raises IndexError or TypeError.

tasks.syntax:
with torch.no_grad():  
    # Operations here execute without autograd graph construction  
    ...

# Or as a function decorator:  
@torch.no_grad()  
def eval_step(inputs):  
    ...
important_params: None.

import torch  
import torch.nn as nn

layer = nn.Linear(5, 1)  
x = torch.randn(3, 5, requires_grad=True)

# Standard tracking  
out_tracked = layer(x)  
print(f"Tracked requires_grad: {out_tracked.requires_grad}")

# Disabled tracking via context manager  
with torch.no_grad():  
    out_untracked = layer(x)

print(f"Untracked requires_grad: {out_untracked.requires_grad}")

Validation and testing loops where gradients are not computed.
Model evaluation steps, batch inference, or writing non-differentiable utility code.
tasks.avoid_when: Real-time production inference on modern PyTorch versions; prefer torch.inference_mode() which offers higher performance.

no_grad() does not switch model operational modes (e.g., Dropout and BatchNorm still behave in training mode unless model.eval() is called explicitly).

tasks.mental_trigger: I want the absolute fastest inference runtime and lowest VRAM overhead possible in modern PyTorch (PyTorch 1.9+ / 2.0+).
tasks.syntax:
with torch.inference_mode():  
    # Optimized inference operations  
    ...

# Or as a function decorator:  
@torch.inference_mode()  
def predict(batch):  
    ...

tasks.example:
import torch  
import torch.nn as nn

class InferenceModel(nn.Module):  
    def __init__(self):  
        super().__init__()  
        self.fc = nn.Linear(10, 2)

    def forward(self, x):  
        return self.fc(x)

model = InferenceModel().eval()  
inputs = torch.randn(4, 10)

# Preferred production inference block  
with torch.inference_mode():  
    predictions = model(inputs)

print(f"Predictions requires_grad: {predictions.requires_grad}")

tasks.avoid_when: Code where returned tensors will later be mutated or used inside a downstream differentiable graph (use torch.no_grad() if tensor views need to re-enter autograd later).
gotchas: Tensors produced within inference_mode cannot participate in autograd later. Mutating them outside the block or using them in tracked graphs raises an error.
inference_mode does not set model.eval(). Remember to call model.eval() to freeze BatchNorm and Dropout layers.

tasks.mental_trigger: I am inside a global no_grad() evaluation loop, but I need to compute gradients for a specific task (e.g., test-time optimization or adversarial attack generation).
tasks.syntax:
with torch.enable_grad():  
    # Operations here track gradients regardless of outer no_grad blocks  
    ...

# Or as a function decorator:  
@torch.enable_grad()  
def compute_adversarial_step(inputs):  
    ...
important_params: None.
tasks.example:
import torch

x = torch.tensor([2.0], requires_grad=True)

@torch.no_grad()  
def evaluation_pipeline(val_tensor):  
    # Outer block has gradients disabled  
    val_res = val_tensor ** 2  
      
    # Temporarily enable gradients for adversarial sampling  
    with torch.enable_grad():  
        x_adv = val_tensor.clone().requires_grad_(True)  
        loss = (x_adv ** 3).sum()  
        loss.backward()  
        adv_grad = x_adv.grad  
          
    return val_res, adv_grad

res, grad = evaluation_pipeline(x)  
print(f"Validation Result (untracked): {res}")  
print(f"Adversarial Gradient (tracked): {grad}")

Generating adversarial examples (e.g., FGSM) during model validation steps.
Executing test-time fine-tuning or meta-learning inner loops inside an overall non-differentiable pipeline.
tasks.avoid_when: Outer contexts already have gradient tracking enabled (redundant).
gotchas: enable_grad cannot override torch.inference_mode(). If enclosed inside an outer inference_mode block, attempting tracking operations will fail or behave unexpectedly; exit inference_mode first.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need to write a custom layer with a specialized derivative, non-differentiable step approximation (e.g., Straight-Through Estimator), or a custom C++/CUDA kernel binding.
important_params: ctx: Context object used to stash arbitrary variables or tensors (ctx.save_for_backward) for consumption during backward.
grad_output: Gradient of loss with respect to the output of this function.
tasks.use_when:
Custom CUDA/C++ extensions lacking native autograd support.
Approximating non-differentiable operations (e.g., binarization, quantization, hard thresholding) with surrogate gradients.
Numerically stabilizing specific sub-networks (e.g., custom log-sum-exp implementations).

gotchas: Saved intermediate non-tensor objects must be stored on ctx directly (e.g., ctx.alpha = alpha). Tensors must be stored using ctx.save_for_backward(tensor1, tensor2) to preserve memory and device tracking.

tasks.task: Detach Tensor from Computation Graph (detach, detach_)
tasks.mental_trigger: I need to stop gradients from flowing back through a specific sub-network or variable while retaining its computed numerical value.
tasks.syntax:
detached_tensor = tensor.detach()  
# Or in-place modification:  
tensor.detach_()
important_params: None.
tasks.example:
import torch

x = torch.tensor([2.0, 3.0], requires_grad=True)

# Derive y with tracking  
y = x ** 2

# Detach y before calculating z  
y_detached = y.detach()  
z = (y_detached * 5).sum()

z.backward()

print(f"x.grad: {x.grad}")  # None, because graph was broken at y_detached  
print(f"y_detached.requires_grad: {y_detached.requires_grad}")

Implementing Actor-Critic reinforcement learning algorithms (e.g., detaching target Q-network targets).
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) where generator and discriminator updates alternate.
Truncated Backpropagation Through Time (TBPTT) in recurrent models.

gotchas: tensor.detach() shares underlying data storage. Modifying detached_tensor in-place will corrupt the original tensor's numerical values, which can cause subtle autograd errors if the original tensor is used in a backward pass.
Using detach() alone does not copy memory. If memory isolation is required, use .clone().detach().

tasks.mental_trigger: I need to call .backward() multiple times on the same loss graph, or compute gradients of gradients (higher-order derivatives).
tasks.syntax: tensor.backward(retain_graph=True, create_graph=True)
important_params: retain_graph (bool): Retains graph execution buffers after computing gradients. Allows calling .backward() again on the same graph without throwing an error.
create_graph (bool): Constructs a computational graph of the backward operations itself, enabling higher-order derivatives (e.g., second derivatives).
tasks.example:
import torch

x = torch.tensor([3.0], requires_grad=True)  
y = x ** 3  # dy/dx = 3x^2 = 27

# First backward: Retain graph buffers and construct higher-order graph  
y.backward(retain_graph=True, create_graph=True)  
first_grad = x.grad.clone()  
print(f"First derivative (dy/dx): {first_grad.item()}")

# Reset x.grad to compute clean second derivative  
x.grad.zero_()

# Calculate second derivative by computing backward on the graph of x.grad  
first_grad.backward()  
print(f"Second derivative (d2y/dx2): {x.grad.item()}")  # d2y/dx2 = 6x = 18
tasks.use_when:
Multi-task learning where multiple task-specific losses are backpropagated sequentially from a shared backbone.
Higher-order derivative algorithms (e.g., Hessian-vector products, MAML meta-learning, WGAN-GP gradient penalties).
tasks.avoid_when: Standard training passes. Setting retain_graph=True unnecessarily causes major VRAM memory leaks.
gotchas: Leaving retain_graph=True active in standard training loops causes memory consumption to increase continuously until the system runs out of memory (OOM).
Using create_graph=True without clearing intermediate states keeps references to backward graphs active, leading to significant memory consumption.

important_params: in_features (int): Size of each input sample.
out_features (int): Size of each output sample.

import torch.nn as nn

linear_layer = nn.Linear(in_features=128, out_features=64)  
x = torch.randn(32, 128)  
output = linear_layer(x)

print(f"Output shape: {output.shape}")
tasks.use_when:
Mapping latent embeddings or extracted features to classification logits.
Building multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs).
Projecting hidden states between transformer layers.
tasks.avoid_when: Processing raw 2D spatial image structures where translation invariance is needed (use nn.Conv2d instead).
gotchas: Input tensor last dimension must match in_features exactly or a RuntimeError will occur.
Initializing heavy nn.Linear modules without device="meta" can exhaust host RAM for massive architectures.
Biases default to Kaiming uniform initialization, which may require manual re-initialization for specific loss landscapes.

bias (bool, optional): If False, the layer will not learn an additive bias. Default: True.

import torch  
import torch.nn as nn

lazy_layer = nn.LazyLinear(out_features=10)

tasks.use_when:
Connecting convolutional trunks to dense heads where calculating flatten dimensions manually is tedious.
Prototyping architectures rapidly.
tasks.avoid_when:
Instantiating optimizers before executing at least one dummy forward pass through the network.
Loading state dicts directly into uninitialized modules.
gotchas: Passing model.parameters() to an optimizer *before* running a forward pass will omit lazy layer parameters from optimization.

Unexpected input shape changes across forward passes after initialization trigger runtime assertion errors.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need to apply sliding filter kernels across sequential data like audio waveforms or time series.
tasks.syntax: torch.nn.Conv1d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size, stride=1, padding=0, dilation=1, groups=1, bias=True, padding_mode='zeros')
important_params: in_channels (int): Number of channels in the input signal.
out_channels (int): Number of channels produced by the convolution.
kernel_size (int or tuple): Size of the convolving kernel.
stride (int or tuple, optional): Stride of the convolution. Default: 1.
padding (int, tuple or str, optional): Zero-padding added to both sides of input. Default: 0.
tasks.example:
import torch  
import torch.nn as nn

conv1d_layer = nn.Conv1d(in_channels=16, out_channels=32, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1)  
# Input shape: Batch=8, Channels=16, Sequence Length=100

output = conv1d_layer(x)

print(f"Output shape: {output.shape}")

tasks.avoid_when: Sequence lengths are highly dynamic and global context is required across long distances without local structure (use Transformers instead).
gotchas: Input shape must strictly follow (Batch, Channels, Length), not (Batch, Length, Channels).
Setting padding='same' is only supported when stride=1.
High dilation values drastically increase memory access footprints without adding parameters.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need sliding 2D kernel filters to extract visual features from multi-channel images.
tasks.syntax: torch.nn.Conv2d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size, stride=1, padding=0, dilation=1, groups=1, bias=True, padding_mode='zeros')
important_params: in_channels (int): Number of channels in the input image.
out_channels (int): Number of channels produced by the convolution.
kernel_size (int or tuple): Size of the convolving kernel.
stride (int or tuple, optional): Stride of the convolution. Default: 1.
padding (int, tuple or str, optional): Padding added to input borders. Default: 0.
tasks.example:
import torch  
import torch.nn as nn

conv2d_layer = nn.Conv2d(in_channels=3, out_channels=64, kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1)  
# Input: Batch=4, RGB Channels=3, Height=224, Width=224  
x = torch.randn(4, 3, 224, 224)  
output = conv2d_layer(x)

print(f"Output shape: {output.shape}")
tasks.use_when: Building vision backbones (e.g., ResNet, YOLO) for image classification, detection, and segmentation tasks.
tasks.avoid_when: Inputs are flat unstructured tabular data vectors.
gotchas: Input shape must be (N, C, H, W) - channels-first layout. Passing channels-last tensors (N, H, W, C) without layout conversion breaks channel math.
Setting groups to in_channels performs depthwise convolution; ensure out_channels is a multiple of in_channels.
Non-matching padding and kernel dimensions can alter spatial resolution unintentionally.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need sliding filters across three dimensions simultaneously (like depth/time, height, and width).
tasks.syntax: torch.nn.Conv3d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size, stride=1, padding=0, dilation=1, groups=1, bias=True, padding_mode='zeros')

import torch.nn as nn

conv3d_layer = nn.Conv3d(in_channels=1, out_channels=16, kernel_size=(3, 3, 3), padding=1)

output = conv3d_layer(x)

print(f"Output shape: {output.shape}")
tasks.use_when: Extracting features from 3D CT/MRI medical scans or processing video sequences with temporal depth.
tasks.avoid_when: Spatial dimensions can be processed frame-by-frame using 2D convolutions with pooled temporal aggregation, saving GPU memory.
gotchas: Extremely high GPU memory usage due to 5D activations; keep batch sizes and channel counts moderate.
Parameter shapes and strides require 3-element tuples if non-square dimensions are used.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need a learnable upsampling layer to increase spatial resolution in decoders or generative models.
tasks.syntax: torch.nn.ConvTranspose2d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size, stride=1, padding=0, output_padding=0, groups=1, bias=True, dilation=1)

out_channels (int): Number of output channels.

import torch

upsample_layer = nn.ConvTranspose2d(in_channels=64, out_channels=32, kernel_size=4, stride=2, padding=1)

output = upsample_layer(x)

print(f"Output shape (doubled resolution): {output.shape}")
tasks.use_when: Decoder architectures in U-Net, Autoencoders, GAN generators, and semantic segmentation heads.
tasks.avoid_when: Avoiding checkerboard artifacts in generated images is crucial (use nn.Upsample followed by nn.Conv2d instead).
gotchas: output_padding is only used to resolve shape ambiguities when stride \> 1; it does not add zero padding to the input itself.
Susceptible to checkerboard artifacts if kernel size is not divisible by stride.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need a standard, fast non-linear activation function that zeroes out negative values.
tasks.syntax: torch.nn.ReLU(inplace=False)
important_params: inplace (bool, optional): If True, modifies the input tensor directly to conserve memory. Default: False.
tasks.example:
import torch  
import torch.nn as nn

relu = nn.ReLU(inplace=True)  
x = torch.tensor([-2.0, -0.5, 0.0, 1.5, 3.0])  
output = relu(x)

print(f"Output: {output}")
tasks.use_when:
Hidden layers in deep convolutional networks and MLPs.
Seeking maximum compute efficiency with zero floating-point transcendental function costs.
tasks.avoid_when: Experiencing "dying ReLU" issues where neurons saturate at 0 permanent gradients during training.
gotchas: Using inplace=True can break Autograd graph computation if the input tensor is needed for gradient calculations in a prior residual path.

tasks.mental_trigger: I want a ReLU activation that prevents inactive neurons from dying by providing a small slope for negative values.
tasks.syntax: torch.nn.LeakyReLU(negative_slope=0.01, inplace=False)
important_params: negative_slope (float, optional): Controls the angle of the negative slope. Default: 0.01.
inplace (bool, optional): Performs operation in-place. Default: False.
tasks.example:
import torch  
import torch.nn as nn

leaky_relu = nn.LeakyReLU(negative_slope=0.1)  
x = torch.tensor([-2.0, -1.0, 0.0, 2.0])  
output = leaky_relu(x)

print(f"Output: {output}")
tasks.use_when: Training deep networks or GAN discriminators prone to dying neuron problems under standard ReLU.
tasks.avoid_when: Canonical architecture specifications explicitly mandate standard ReLU or GELU activations.
gotchas: Setting negative_slope too high converts the layer into a near-linear transformation.
Inplace operations can cause backpropagation graph issues in complex computational DAGs.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need the standard smooth activation function used in modern Transformer architectures like BERT and GPT.
tasks.syntax: torch.nn.GELU(approximate='none')
important_params: approximate (str, optional): Approximation algorithm to use ('none' or 'tanh'). Default: 'none'.

import torch  
import torch.nn as nn

gelu = nn.GELU(approximate='tanh')  
x = torch.randn(2, 4)  
output = gelu(x)

print(f"Output:\\n{output}")
tasks.use_when: Constructing modern Transformer Feed-Forward Networks (FFN) and Vision Transformers (ViT).
tasks.avoid_when: Deploying on ultra-low-power edge hardware lacking fast transcendental GPU kernel implementations.
gotchas: Setting approximate='tanh' produces slight numerical differences compared to 'none'. Ensure consistency across training and inference engines.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need a smooth, non-monotonic activation function used in state-of-the-art vision backbones like EfficientNet and YOLO.

import torch.nn as nn

tasks.use_when: Implementing modern vision models (e.g., YOLOv8, EfficientNet, ConvNeXt) or LLM architectures (e.g., LLaMA SwiGLU blocks).
tasks.avoid_when: Strict compatibility with legacy edge devices that accelerate plain ReLU only is required.
gotchas: Inplace SiLU (inplace=True) requires modern PyTorch versions to compute backward passes correctly without memory allocation conflicts.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need to convert raw unnormalized logits into categorical class probability values along a specific dimension.

important_params: dim (int): The dimension along which Softmax will be computed. (Triggers warning if omitted).
tasks.example:
import torch  
import torch.nn as nn

softmax = nn.Softmax(dim=-1)  
logits = torch.tensor([[2.0, 1.0, 0.1], [0.5, 3.0, 1.2]])

print(f"Sum across dimension: {probs.sum(dim=-1)}")

tasks.avoid_when: Training multiclass classifiers using nn.CrossEntropyLoss (which expects raw, unnormalized logits directly).
gotchas: Applying Softmax prior to nn.CrossEntropyLoss causes severe numerical instability and poor gradient propagation during training.
Forgetting to specify dim leads to implicit fallback warnings in PyTorch.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need log-probabilities from raw network logits to use with negative log-likelihood loss (nn.NLLLoss).

important_params: dim (int): Dimension along which LogSoftmax is computed.

import torch  
import torch.nn as nn

log_softmax = nn.LogSoftmax(dim=1)  
logits = torch.randn(3, 5)  
log_probs = log_softmax(logits)

print(f"Log Probabilities shape: {log_probs.shape}")

tasks.avoid_when: Model output feeds directly into nn.CrossEntropyLoss.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need spatial dimension reduction that preserves dominant salient features while introducing small translation invariance.

stride (int or tuple, optional): Stride of the window. Defaults to kernel_size.

import torch  
import torch.nn as nn

pool = nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2)  
x = torch.randn(1, 16, 32, 32)  
output = pool(x)

print(f"Downsampled shape: {output.shape}")

tasks.avoid_when: Information loss from dropping non-maximum spatial values degrades task performance (e.g., fine-grained segmentation).

tasks.mental_trigger: I want to downsample spatial feature maps smoothly without overemphasizing extreme max activation spikes.
tasks.syntax: torch.nn.AvgPool2d(kernel_size, stride=None, padding=0, ceiling_mode=False, count_include_pad=True, divisor_override=None)

stride (int or tuple, optional): Stride of window. Defaults to kernel_size.
padding (int or tuple, optional): Implicit zero padding. Default: 0.
count_include_pad (bool, optional): Includes zero-padding in the averaging calculation. Default: True.
tasks.example:
import torch  
import torch.nn as nn

avg_pool = nn.AvgPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2)  
x = torch.randn(1, 8, 16, 16)  
output = avg_pool(x)

print(f"Output shape: {output.shape}")

tasks.avoid_when: Extracting sharp, localized target features (e.g., text or distinct edge signals in images).
gotchas: Setting count_include_pad=True skews border average values downwards due to padded zeros.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need to reduce spatial feature maps to a fixed output size (e.g., 1×1) for variable-sized input images.
tasks.syntax: torch.nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(output_size)
important_params: output_size (int or tuple): Target output spatial size (H_out, W_out) or a single integer H_out for (H_out, H_out). None retains original dimension size.

import torch  
import torch.nn as nn

# Global Average Pooling (1x1 output target)  
gap = nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d((1, 1))  
x_large = torch.randn(2, 512, 14, 14)  
x_small = torch.randn(2, 512, 7, 7)

print(f"Large input output: {gap(x_large).shape}")  
print(f"Small input output: {gap(x_small).shape}")

tasks.avoid_when: Strict layout preservation of precise sub-region spatial indices is required.
gotchas: Non-divisible target output shapes relative to input shapes can cause non-uniform window bin sizes across spatial edges.

tasks.mental_trigger: I want fixed-size feature maps via max extraction across variable input image dimensions.
tasks.syntax: torch.nn.AdaptiveMaxPool2d(output_size, return_indices=False)
important_params: output_size (int or tuple): Target output spatial dimensions (H_out, W_out).
return_indices (bool, optional): If True, returns max pixel index locations along with output values. Default: False.
tasks.example:
import torch  
import torch.nn as nn

adaptive_max_pool = nn.AdaptiveMaxPool2d((2, 2))  
x = torch.randn(1, 64, 15, 19)  
output = adaptive_max_pool(x)

print(f"Output shape fixed at 2x2: {output.shape}")
tasks.use_when: Creating spatial pyramid pooling (SPP) networks requiring fixed-length feature vectors across varied input spatial ratios.
tasks.avoid_when: Smooth feature aggregation is required (prefer nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d).
gotchas: Input spatial dimensions smaller than specified output target sizes produce runtime shape errors or duplicated pixel samples.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need to reduce internal covariate shift across mini-batches in convolutional or dense architectures.
tasks.syntax: torch.nn.BatchNorm2d(num_features, eps=1e-05, momentum=0.1, affine=True, track_running_stats=True)
important_params: num_features (int): Number of channels *C* expected in the input tensor.
eps (float, optional): Value added to the denominator for numerical stability. Default: 1e-5.
momentum (float, optional): Value used for the running_mean and running_var computation. Default: 0.1.
affine (bool, optional): If True, enables learnable gamma scale and beta shift parameters. Default: True.
track_running_stats (bool, optional): If True, tracks running mean and running variance. Default: True.
tasks.example:
import torch  
import torch.nn as nn

bn = nn.BatchNorm2d(num_features=64)  
bn.train() # Enable batch stat tracking  
x = torch.randn(8, 64, 32, 32)  
output = bn(x)

print(f"Normalized output shape: {output.shape}")
tasks.use_when: Standard deep vision backbones (ResNets, ConvNets) with batch sizes ≥16.
tasks.avoid_when: Micro-batch sizes (*N*≤4) or variable sequence lengths (use nn.LayerNorm or nn.GroupNorm instead).
gotchas: Forgetting to call model.eval() causes inference inputs to update running statistics and produce inaccurate results.
Single-sample batches (*N*=1) during training mode trigger runtime errors when calculating sample variance.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need normalization that operates per-sample, making it invariant to mini-batch sizes (crucial for Transformers and RNNs).
tasks.syntax: torch.nn.LayerNorm(normalized_shape, eps=1e-05, elementwise_affine=True, bias=True, device=None, dtype=None)
important_params: normalized_shape (int or list/tuple): Input shape from an expected trailing dimension (e.g., [hidden_dim]).
eps (float, optional): Numerical stability offset. Default: 1e-5.
elementwise_affine (bool, optional): If True, learns scale and shift parameters. Default: True.
tasks.example:
import torch  
import torch.nn as nn

batch_size, seq_len, hidden_dim = 4, 128, 768  
ln = nn.LayerNorm(hidden_dim)

x = torch.randn(batch_size, seq_len, hidden_dim)  
output = ln(x)

print(f"LayerNorm output shape: {output.shape}")
tasks.use_when: Transformer architectures, sequence models, and small mini-batch workloads.
tasks.avoid_when: Standard convolutional layers where spatial-channel coupling benefits more from nn.BatchNorm or nn.GroupNorm.
gotchas: normalized_shape must align precisely with the trailing dimensions of the input tensor.

tasks.mental_trigger: I want batch-size independent channel normalization for visual models where BatchNorm fails due to small batch sizes.
tasks.syntax: torch.nn.GroupNorm(num_groups, num_channels, eps=1e-05, affine=True, device=None, dtype=None)
important_params: num_groups (int): Number of groups to divide channels into.
num_channels (int): Total number of channels in input tensors.
eps (float, optional): Stability additive epsilon. Default: 1e-5.
affine (bool, optional): If True, learns scale and shift weights. Default: True.
tasks.example:
import torch  
import torch.nn as nn

# Divide 32 channels into 4 groups (8 channels per group)  
gn = nn.GroupNorm(num_groups=4, num_channels=32)  
x = torch.randn(2, 32, 64, 64)  
output = gn(x)

print(f"GroupNorm output shape: {output.shape}")
tasks.use_when: Training high-resolution visual tasks (e.g., object detection, segmentation) forced to run at small batch sizes (*N*≤4).
tasks.avoid_when: Large batch size training regimes where standard nn.BatchNorm2d achieves superior accuracy.
gotchas: num_channels must be strictly divisible by num_groups.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need normalization that strips instance-specific style and contrast variations from images (e.g., for style transfer or image translation).
tasks.syntax: torch.nn.InstanceNorm2d(num_features, eps=1e-05, momentum=0.1, affine=False, track_running_stats=False)
important_params: num_features (int): Number of channels *C*.
affine (bool, optional): Enables learnable affine parameters. Default: False (unlike BatchNorm).
track_running_stats (bool, optional): Tracks global statistics. Default: False.
tasks.example:
import torch  
import torch.nn as nn

norm = nn.InstanceNorm2d(num_features=16, affine=True)  
x = torch.randn(2, 16, 32, 32)  
output = norm(x)

print(f"Output shape: {output.shape}")
tasks.use_when: Generative tasks, neural style transfer, and image-to-image translation models (e.g., CycleGAN).
tasks.avoid_when: Standard image classification where preserving overall luminance/contrast variance is helpful.
gotchas: affine defaults to False in InstanceNorm2d, whereas it defaults to True in BatchNorm2d.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need a strong, standard regularization layer to mitigate neural network overfitting.
tasks.syntax: torch.nn.Dropout(p=0.5, inplace=False)
important_params: p (float, optional): Probability of an element being zeroed. Default: 0.5.
inplace (bool, optional): Performs operation in-place. Default: False.

import torch  
import torch.nn as nn

drop = nn.Dropout(p=0.3)  
x = torch.ones(1, 10)

drop.train()  
print(f"Training mode output (scaled & dropped):\\n{drop(x)}")

drop.eval()  
print(f"Eval mode output (pass-through):\\n{drop(x)}")
tasks.use_when: Training densely connected layers or transformer hidden blocks prone to memorization.
tasks.avoid_when:
Performing evaluation/inference (eval() mode must be explicitly invoked).
Normalizing 2D convolutional feature maps (prefer nn.Dropout2d).
gotchas: Forgetting to toggle model.eval() keeps dropout active during inference, causing non-deterministic prediction outputs.

tasks.mental_trigger: I need spatial regularization for 2D convolutional feature maps where adjacent spatial pixels are highly correlated.
tasks.syntax: torch.nn.Dropout2d(p=0.5, inplace=False)
important_params: p (float, optional): Probability of a channel being zeroed out. Default: 0.5.
inplace (bool, optional): Modifies tensor in-place. Default: False.
tasks.example:
import torch  
import torch.nn as nn

spatial_drop = nn.Dropout2d(p=0.4)  
spatial_drop.train()  
# Input: Batch=1, Channels=4, Height=4, Width=4  
x = torch.ones(1, 4, 4, 4)  
output = spatial_drop(x)

# Entire 2D channel maps are zeroed out together  
print(f"Zeroed channels sample output:\\n{output[0, :, 0, 0]}")
tasks.use_when: Regularizing deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) where standard pixel-level dropout is ineffective due to spatial auto-correlation.
tasks.avoid_when: Processing 1D sequential inputs or flat dense layers.
gotchas: Input tensor must have at least 3 dimensions (N, C, L) or 4 dimensions (N, C, H, W).

tasks.mental_trigger: I want to chain linear feed-forward network layers together simply without writing explicit forward code for each step.

torch.nn.Sequential(*args)

torch.nn.Sequential(OrderedDict([('name', module), ...]))

import torch.nn as nn

mlp = nn.Sequential(  
    nn.Linear(784, 128),  
    nn.ReLU(),  
    nn.Dropout(0.2),
